[Diaporthe] Symptoms:
Diaporthe on soybean exhibits distinctive symptoms primarily on stems, leaves, and pods, characterized by dark brown to black lesions that are typically sunken and have raised margins. These lesions can vary in size and shape but often present as irregular patches ranging from a few millimeters to several centimeters in diameter. Affected tissues may show a discolored, leathery appearance, with some areas exhibiting a glossy, dark coating of mycelium at high humidity conditions. Occasionally, small, pinpoint black pycnidia can emerge at the center of the lesions, contributing to a spotted appearance. Leaf symptoms may manifest as angular lesions bordered by yellow halos, while pod infections can lead to shrivelled seeds and reduced quality. This disease can also cause wilting and premature death of infected tissues, giving plants a scorched look. Unlike Phomopsis, which features smaller, more uniform lesions predominantly on leaves, Diaporthe lesions display irregular shapes and are more pervasive across various plant parts. | Often confused with: Diaporthe_2015_Kanawha

[Phomopsis] Symptoms:
Phomopsis in soybeans presents as small, dark brown to black lesions on leaves, which may appear sunken and are typically oval or irregular in shape, ranging from 1 to 3 mm in diameter. These lesions often exhibit a lighter brown or yellow halo at their periphery, surrounded by healthy tissue, indicating localized tissue damage. Infected pods can develop elongated, dark streaks or galls that may lead to premature pod drop, while stems may show streaking with a rough texture. Affected parts often have a dry, necrotic appearance, and upon close inspection, signs of black pycnidia may be visible within the lesions, producing a dark speckled effect. Symptoms are generally distributed randomly throughout the lower canopy of the plant, contributing to a patchy appearance across fields. A key difference between Phomopsis and the visually similar disease of Septoria is that Phomopsis lesions lack the prominent chlorotic halos commonly seen in Septoria-infected leaves.

[Diaporthe_2015_Kanawha] Symptoms:
Diaporthe 2015 Kanawha manifests in soybeans primarily through dark brown to black lesions that appear as elongated, sunken spots on stems and leaf petioles, often accompanied by a distinctive taupe halo. These lesions are typically surrounded by discolored tissue displaying shades of yellow to orange, indicative of tissue stress. The lesions can vary in size, commonly measuring 3 to 10 mm in length, and are frequently scattered irregularly along the plant, leading to a noticeable linear pattern. In severe cases, black, raised fruiting bodies may emerge from these lesions, contributing to the overall textural roughness of the affected areas. Symptoms can extend to the pods, where dark galls form and spoil the seeds inside, while the leaves may demonstrate premature wilting and curling. In contrast to Tanspot, which presents as superficial circular lesions with clear margins predominantly on the leaves, Diaporthe lesions are more pronounced on woody stems and exhibit sunken characteristics, making this disease visually identifiable by its raised fruiting structures and distribution across various plant parts. | Often confused with: Diaporthe
